347. "We started our fight to liberate Vurungamari from the Pakistani occupa-tion forces on November 11, 1971. On November 13 we came near the outskirts of Vurungamari, and the Indian Air Force intensified their air attack. On November 14 morning the guns from the Pakistani side fell silent and we entered Vurungamari with shouts of "Joy Bangla" (Victory to Bangladesh).

 

348. But I still did not anticipate the ter-rible scene I was gOing to witness as we were heading toward east of Vurungamari to take up our positions. I was informed by wireless to go to the Circle Officer's office. After we reached the office, we caught glimpses of several young women through the windows of the second floor. After breaking down the door of the room, where the women were kept, we were dumbfounded. We found four naked young women, who had been physically tortured, raped, and battered by the Pakistani soldiers. We immediately came out of the room and threw in four Lungis [dresses] and four bed-sheets for them to cover themselves. We tried to talk to them, butall of them were still in shock. One of them was six to seven-months pregnant. One was a college student froth Mymensingh. We found many dead bodies and skeletons in the bushes along the road. Many of the skeletons had long hair and had on torn Saris and Bangles on their hands. We found sixteen other women locked up in a room at Vurungamari High School. These women were brought in for Pakistani soldiers from nearby villages. We found evidence in the rooms of the Circle Officers office which showed that these women were tied to the window bars and were repeatedly raped by the Pakistani soldiers. The whole floor was covered with blood, torn pieces of clothing and strands of long hair."

 

THE OFFICER'S WIFE

 

349. This testimony is from Anita Malik's "The Year of the Vulture."

 

350. "Another pathetic case is that of a woman of about 25. I-Ter husband was a government officer in a Sub-division and she had three children. They first took away the husband, although she cried and pleaded with them. Then they returned him half-dead, after brutal torture. Then another lot of soldiers came in at 8 or 9 A.M. and raped her in front of her husband and children. They tied up the husband and hit the children when they cried.

 

351. Then another lot of soldier came at 2.30 PM and took her away. They kept her in a bunker and used to rape her every night until she became senseless. When she returned after three months, she was pregnant. The villagers were very sympathetic about her but the husband refused to take her back. When the villagers kept pressuring him to take her back, he hanged himself. She is now in an advanced stage of pregnancy and we are doing all that we can do to help her. But she is inconsolable. But why, why did they do it? It would have been better if we had both died."

 

352. The present case is one of the instances what Pakistani solders and their collaborators did in this country in 1971 in the name of security of United Pakistan. We have found in this charge how the Pakistan army and this appellant dealt with an innocent village woman. A number of soldiers committed rape upon an unfortunate woman, one after another. From the evidence, we cannot come to any other conclusion except the one that the victim P.W.5 Majeda Begum was abducted at the instance of the appellant and the appellant himself handed her over to Pakistan army only for the reason that she was brother's daughter of Abdul Matin, a veteran freedom fighter. Motive of abducting P.W.5 Majeda Begum and handing over her to Pak army was deliberate so that Pak army could rape her and Pak army did so fulfilling the desire of the appellant. It is the duty of tribunal to award proper sentence and it did it. Involvement in such brutality and cruelty in any manner is a crime against humanity. The P.W.5 shall never be able to remove such harrowing and traumatic memory till her last breath. It was the duty of the civilised society to put the person / persons responsible for such occurrence on trial and same was done in this case.

 

Charge No.13

 

353. "That on 18 August 1971 in between 09:00-09:30 am and 03:00-03:30 pm a group of 15-20 Razakars and peace committee members led by accused Syed Md. Qaiser by launching attack apprehended Abdus Shahid and three other civilians of village Narapati under police station Chunarughat district Habiganj and brought them to peace committee office set up at the house, of Rajendra Poddar @ Lichu Poddar where on appellant's instruction they were subjected to torture and forced to disclose information about the arms they had. At a stage of causing torture, they were brought to army camp, one mile far from the peace committee office and then the accused and the group brought the detained persons to the killing filed adjacent to Nalua tea garden by army vehicle where they were killed. Therefore, accused Syed Md. Qaiser has been charged for participating, abetting, facilitating and contributing the actual commission of killing of 03 unarmed civilians constituting the offence of 'murder as crime against humanity' which was part of attack against civilian population as specified in section 3(2)(a)(g)(h) of the Act which are punishable under section 20(2) read with section 3(1) of the Act. And thus the accused incurred liability under section 4(1) of the Act."

 

354. From charge No.13, it appears that allegations brought against the appellant was that he participated, abetted, facilitated and contributed the Pakistani army in killing Abdus Saheed and 3 other civilians at Nalua tea garden after abducting them from village Narapati.

 

355. In support of this charge, the prosecution examined 2(two) witnesses who are P.W.23 Ambia Khatun and P.W.24 Anowara Begum.

 

356. P.W. 23 Ambia Khatun in her testimony stated that after Fazar prayer, first Bhadra, 1971 her father knocked the door of their dwelling hut. Accordingly, her mother opened the door. Her father and two others namely, Jahir Hossain, Mahibullah entered into their dwelling but and their friend Askor Ali left therefrom for his house. After some times, Askor Ali returned to the house of P.W. 23. At about 8 /9 p.m., Feroz Miah (Vice Chairman), Esad Ali, Monfar, Moslem Chairman, Hurai Chowkider and Khaleque Chowkidar surrounded their house and directed the victims to come out from the house. When her father asked them about the cause of such calling, they replied that Syed Qaiser had called those victims in the house of Lichu Poddar where he was waiting. Thereafter, they, confining those 4 (four) victims, left the place towards the house of Lichu Poddar. Mother, grandmother, uncle, wife of Askar Ali and this witness herself followed them but raiding parties did not allow them to enter into the house of Lichu Poddar. They started waiting near a latrine and found the appellant Qaiser inside that house who interrogated those victims since they had returned from India. The appellant asked his bahini to fasten those victims and to start assaulting.

 

357. The members of Qaiser bahini started assaulting the victims. Looking at the severity of assault, this witness started crying. At the relevant time, the appellant, wearing white coloured pant and shirt and a cap on the head, passed the order to assault the victims. Thereafter, Qaiser and other members of his bahini, taking the victims, went towards north side of Mazar of Shah Gadar Hossain. This witness heard that the victims were handed over to Pakistani army personel. One Hamdu Razakar disclosed that those victims had been killed. This witness and other inmates started crying. Hamdu Razakar told that the victims were killed under a tree of Nalua Tea Garden and killing squad had thrown their dead bodies in a well. Hamdu Razakar also disclosed that Syed Qaiser ordered Hamdu Razakar to kill the victims who denied. Thus, pursuant to the order of Qaiser, Pakistani army personnel had killed the victims. Sometimes thereafter, her husband went to the house of victim Shaheed. This witness also went to the house of Shaheed and requested her husband to get him returned to their house. 359. Mr. S.M. Shahjahan, learned Advocate appearing for the appellant, submits that the P.Ws.23 and 24 are not the witnesses of occurrence of killing of those victims, the conviction awarded to the appellant on the basis of the testimony of hearsay evidence is unsafe, the Tribunal committed error of law in convicting the appellant on the basis of testimony of hearsay witnesses.

 

360. Mr. Mahbubey Aldm, learned Attorney General appearing for the respondent, submits that this two witnesses are the eye witnesses of the occurrence of abduction and assault of the victims which were done at the instance of the appellant; the Tribunal rightly convicted the appellant.

Sometimes thereafter, Razakar bahini surrounded their house and confined them and compelled them to go to the house of Lichu Poddar. This witness followed them and witnessed the occurrence of assaulting the victims by the members of the appellants bahini pursuant to the order of the appellant in, the house of Lichu Poddar. Her testimony was fully corroborated by P.W.24 Anowara Begum. She also witnessed the act of abduction of those victims by the members of appellants bahini and she herself saw the occurrence of assaulting the victims pursuant to the order given by the appellant. That is, the P.Ws. 23 and 24 corroborated each other as to the material particulars. In the house of Lichu Poddar they found the appellant Qaiser who interrogated the victims' and passed the order to the members of his bahini to assault the victims. In the evening, these two witnesses heard that the victims had been killed. They rushed to the place of occurrence of Nalua Tea Garden, the people present there told them that the victims were killed and their dead bodies were thrown in a well. In view of the facts, circumstances and evidence on record, we do not find any wrong in the judgment of the tribunal in respect of this charge.

 

362. Accordingly, we are of the view that Tribunal rightly convicted and sentenced the appellant in this charge.

364. It appears from the Charge No.14, that the appellant, his bahini and Pakistani army personnel, abducting victims Akkas Ali, Abdus Sattar, Ohed Ali and Seraj Ali of village- Mouzpur, killed them, and thereafter, they threw dead bodies in the river Sonai.

From the testimonies of P.Ws: 26 and 27, it appears that the victims were confined from the house. of P.W. 27 by the appellant's bahini and, thereafter, the killing squad brought them at Jagadishpur High School army camp where the appellant himself tortured the victims and then they brought the victims to the bank of river Sonai and the appellant gave signal to kill the victims. Charge No.16

Azaharul Huq in his testimony stated that on 15th November, 1971 at about 8/9 a.m. he saw by his binocular that `Qaiser bahini', Razakar bahini and members of Pakistani army, entering into the villages started firing abruptly. 380. Mr. S.M. Shahjahan appearing on behalf of the appellant, submits that the P.W. 1 and 13 are not the eye witnesses of the occurrence. P.W. 3 was an accomplice of the appellant and his evidence has got no probativewalue. The evidence of P.W. 31 Md. Azaharul Huq is unreliable. The conviction relying upon the testimony of P.W.16 is unsafe.

 

381. Mr. Mahbubey Alam, learned Attorney General appearing on behalf respondent, submits that P.Ws.3, 16 and 31 are eyewitnesses of the occurrence and in different books material exhibit-E, namely মুক্তিযুদ্ধে স্বারক চিত্রে, material exhibit-Ja সিলেট গণহত্যা material exhibit Jha মুক্তিযুদ্ধের ইতিহাসের খোঁজে it was mentioned that the appellant was present at the time of commission of atrocities in 22 different villages under Nasirnagar Police Station. He submits that the tribunal has not committed any error in relying upon the testimonies of P.Ws.3, 16 and 31 and convicted the appellant in this charge.

 

382. From the testimony of P.W.3 it appears that he was a member of the appellant's bahini and he himself participated in the occurrence committed on 15.11.1971. He categorically stated that appellant Qaiser, his bahini and Pakistani army were responsible for the brutal killings, assaulting and arsoning dated 15.11.1971. Testimony of this witness also proved that the appellant conspired to commit genocide in the above named villages. P.W. 16 Abdul Matin, had been able to identify the appellant at the time of commission of offence committed in the aforesaid villages hiding himself in jungle and field of crops. He saw that, at one stage, appellant Qaiser and his bahini dividing themselves in two groups attacked two villages at a time. This witness saw some dead bodies of the unfortunate victims of those villages and heard that about 108 unarmed civilians were killed at the time of commission of atrocities. P.W.31 Md. Aaharul Huq in his testimony stated that he also saw the appellant at the time of commission of occurrence in those villages on 15.11.1971. We have gone through the evidence of P.W.3, 16 and 31, we do not find any inconsistency in their testimonies as to the presence and participation of the appellant in the occurrence dated 15.11.1971 and, thus the conclusion arrived at by the Tribunal that the appellant himself and his bahini along with the members of Pakistan army attacked aforesaid villages and killed 108 unarmed civilians is based on evidence. The evidence is quite overwhelming as to the time, place and manner of brutality committed on 15.11.1971 and the Tribunal rightly convicted and sentenced the appellant in, Charge No.16 believing the testimonies of P.W.3 Tazul Islam, P.W.16 Abdul Matin and P.W.31 Md. Azaharul Huq. It was deliberate widespread and systematic killings of a large group of unarmed civilians which was the gravest crime against humanity. The descriptions of killings given in the produced books supported the prosecution case. This was a holocaust in which more than one hundred unarmed civilians were systematically killed. The civilian population areas were intentionally targeted by the brute Pakistan army and the appellant's "Qaiser bahini". The prosecution has been able to prove that the appellant participated, abetted, aided and assisted in the commission of crimes against humanity committed in the villages Daora, Nichintapur, Korgoan, Burungi, Citna, Alogpur, Laxmipur etc. under Nasirnagor Police Station on 15.11.1971. It was violence against members of a national and religious group with the intent to destroy the entire group. It was the deliberate and systematic destruction of a group of people because of their nationality and religion.

 

383. Documentary and oral evidence, adduced by the prosecution have revealed that the appellant formed a killing squad in the name of "Qaiser bahini" and launched attacks upon the unarmed civilians. It was, in fact, "seizure of power" by the appellant's Qaiser bahini. It is the case of the prosecution that the Qaiser bahini was a criminal organization. It was involved in the systematic, widespread murders, arsoning, looting, torturing, rape and ill-treatment of the Civilian populations. Qaiser bahini was used for commission of offences against humanity defined under the ICT Act.

CONCLUDING CHAPTER.

 

385. On perusal of the evidence it appears that the evidence against the appellant relating to war crimes are overwhelming in its volume and details. The killing, torturing, confining, abduction and other inhuman acts upon civilian populations reached its highest. There is no doubt from reading of the evidence that the criminal acts described in the indictments were widespread and systematic attacks against civilian population. The appellant participated, aided and abetted numerous acts of inhuman torturing, killings, arsoning and looting during war of liberation. It is relevant here to quote two passage from our observations made in the case of Mir Quasem Ali Vs. The Chief Prosecutor reported in 2 LM (AD) 364 which are:

 

386. "Let us now consider whether there is any direct involvement of the accused in support of the charge. It is to be noted that the incidents of offences of the nature have been perpetrated about 42 years before the trial has taken place. It is one of the challenging task to collect legal evidence because of the changes during this intervening period, but also the fact that most of the witnesses are not alive. More so, in the intervening period, the political scenario had been changed after the killing of Bangabandhu Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. The regime which came to power rehabilitated the anti-liberation forces and the persons who perpetrated these crimes against humanity were also accommodated in the government. Those perpetrators perpetrated crimes against humanity in a similar manner. They not only screen out the legal evidence but als6 distorted the history of the liberation struggle lest their abhorrent roles are known by the young generation. This has done by the defeatdd forces of the First World War and the Nazis in the second world wars, even thereafter, in Cambodia, Khemr Rouge regime of Polpot, Tatsis in Rwanda, Serbian forces in Bosnia etc. The court can take judicial notice of this common practice from the history. In our country the admitted position is that some right wing political parties with direct cooperation and participation of the perpetrators remained in power from 1975 and destroyed, destructed, and defaced almost all legal evidence in a planned manner.

 

387. It is, therefore, sufficient to convict an accused person charged with offences of crimes against humanity if it is proved that the offender has some knowledge of, and sympathy for the inhumane policy so as to give him a mental 'element more culpable than that of the ordinary offender. This principle has followed in other regions of the globe where similar crimes have been committed. In some cases it has been held that if an offender merely awares that his crime is also being committed by others in a wide-spread basis, he may be held guilty of the offence. The expression 'awareness' must be taken to include some approval of policy, as for example, in Dusko Tadic case, the accused was a local thug who was allowed to enter occasionally to torture prisoners. He was implicated in the ethnic cleansing of his village, by calling out Muslim civilians from houses, forcibly separating the women and children and elderly from the older men, and dispatching them to different camps. The tribunal held that this behaviour amounted to a crime against humanity compendiously described as 'persecution', namely, repeated inhuman acts of harassment, torment, oppression and discrimination intended to Cause suffering and inflicted because the victims belong to a different ethic group from their persecutors. The Judges are at one end of the spectrum, exercising a power to persuade which foot soldiers like Tadic, at the other end, actually put into practice-all are guilty; their responsibility as individuals may differ in degree, but not in kind. (Crimes Against Humanity by Geoffrey Robertson. P 316-317)."

 

388. From the evidence it appears to us that the prosecution has been able to prove that the appellant himself formed a killing squad named "Qaiser Bahini" and he became commander of that bahini and had superior command over his force. The defence was given sufficient opportunity to disprove the charge of the command position of the appellant but he failed to disprove the same. His bahini acted as death squad. In Mir Quasems Case (supra) we have also observed: "Sub-section (2) is altogether different and if any commander or superior officer under whose command any one of his force commits any of the crimes described in section 3 or is connected with any plans or fails to discharge his duty to maintain discipline or who fails to control or supervise the actions of his persons under his command and if the subordinates or any one of them commits any such crime, he will be guilty of such crimes. If the superior officer participates in any of the crimes mentioned above, he cannot escape from superior responsibility because of the fact that his responsibility is to prevent his subordinates to commit crimes. The commander is responsible for failure to perform an act required by law. This omission is culpable because law imposes a responsibility to prevent and punish crimes committed by his subordinatei Even if it is proved that he did not participate but his subordinates committed the offence within his knowledge or that he has prepared a plan to commit any of the offences, in that ease also, he cannot avoid the responsibility because law imposes a responsibility on the part of a commander or superior officer to shoulder the responsibility for commission of any crimes committed by his subordinates."

 

389. From the facts, circumstances and evidence adduced by the prosecution it is proved that the appellant was involved in deliberate and systematic destruction and killing of unarmed Bengali civilians and was also involved in aiding, planning, contributing and abetting the Pakistan army who committed genocide and crimes against humanity with an object to wipeout in whole or in part of Bengali nation.

 

390. ICTY, in Prosecutor V. Tihomir Blaskic, IT-95-14-T, Prosecutor V. Vlado Kupreski. IT-95-16, Prosecutor V. Dusko Tadic, 11-94-1-1 and Prosecutor V. Fatmir Llmay-IT-03-66-T, observed that the term civilian is broadly interpreted to mean a population which is predominantly civilian because of its non-combatant status as being largely innocent. It was further observed that the presence of non-civilians, such as the members of armed resistance groups or former combatants who have laid down their arms, does not alter the civilian character of the population, which remains predominantly civilian in nature despite the presence of few non civilians. There is no requirement nor is it an element of crimes against humanity that the victims of the underling crimes be "civilians" or even be predominantly civilians, provided the acts form part of a widespread or systematic attacks directed against a civilian population.

 

391. According to section 3(2)(b) of the ICT Act, 1973 genocide includes any of the following acts: (i) killing members of the group (ii) causing serious bodily or mental harm to members of the group (iii) deliberately inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part. United Nations General Assembly while defining genocide observed that many instances of such crimes of genocide have occurred when racial, religious, political and other groups have been destroyed entirely or in part and whether the crimes is committed on religious, racial political or any other grounds. It is the crime of crimes and its intentional basis should be to destroy a group and it should target and least a substantial number or part of that group. In Randovan Karadzic and Ratko Mladic Review of Indictment pursuant to Rule 61, IT-95-5R61 and IT 18-R61 observed that genocide may be inferred from the very gravity of acts, which inclusively include: uniform methods used in committing the said crimes. Their pattern, their pervasiveness throughout all of the Bosnian Serb-held territory, the movements between the various camps, and the terror of some of the accused's statements were strong indications of genocidal intent. The ICTY and ICTR appeals chambers have held that there is no need to establish a "plan" to commit genocide. This means it is possible to prove the commission of genocide without any evidence of involvement by a state or by a state like entity. According to Appeals chamber of the ICTY, "The act of killing under genocide, consists of three material elements, the victim is dead , the death resulted from an unlawful act or omission of the perpetrator or a subordinate, and at the time of killing, the accused or a subordinate had the intention to kill or inflict grievous bodily harm on the deceased knowing that such bodily harm is likely to cause the victim's death or is reckless about whether the death ensues or not ( Prosecutor Vs. Akayesh, Case ICTR-96-4-T)."

 

392. Out of the indictments brought against the appellant, the prosecution has been able to prove two charges in respect of crimes of rape and sexual violence. In ICT Act, 1973 includes rape as one of the components of crimes against humanity. Rape is a violent and torturous act that severs the personal dignity of victims in a humiliating and contemptuous manner. Rape and forced pregnancy are crimes against humanity and genocide as well since those involve the unlawful confinement of woman forcibly made pregnant which caused serious bodily and mental harm. The appellant had direct involvement of con-fining and abducting P.W.5 Majeda Begom and, thereafter, handing over her to Pakistan army. In spite of repeated request of her father and uncle he did not release Majeda. He knew very well about the fate of Majeda in army custody. He knew very well that Pakistan army dragged off thousands of such daughters of Bengal into sexual violence, rape and forced pregnancy which was crimes against humanity.

 

393. There have been hundreds of "Mylaies and Liddices" in Bangladesh due to the atrocities committed by Pakistan army. It was a tragedy for the entire world' community. The appellant himself was a witness of brutality and massacres of Bengali civilians committed by Pakistan army but without helping the helpless Bengalis he, forming a special bahini named "Qaiser bahini" participated in the crimes against Humanity and genocide and aided, abet-ted and facilitated the Pakistan army to commit such crimes. In Prosecutor V. Kamubanda, Case No. 1CTR-95-54-T-(Trial Chamber) it was observed that the principle that criminal responsibility for any crime in the statute is incurred not only by individuals who physically commit that crime, but also by individuals who participate in and contribute to the commission of a crime in other ways, ranging from its initial planning to its execution, as specified in the five categories of acts, namely, planning, instigating, ordering, committing or aiding and abetting. In the case of Semanza V. Prosecutor, Case No. ICTR-97-20A (Appeal Chamber), it was observed that for an accused to be convicted as perpetrator or co-perpetrator of genocide, it is not necessary that he or she fulfills a "key coordinating role" or that a "high level genocidal plan' be established even if the existence of a plan to commit genocide can be useful to prove the specific intent required for genocide. In the case of aiding and abetting no proof is required of the existence of a common concerted plan. No plan or agreement is required, indeed, the principal may not even know about the accomplice's contribution. The aider and abettor carries out acts specifically directed to assist, encourage or lend moral support to the perpetration of a certain specific crime and this support has a substantial effect upon the perpetration of the crime.

 

394. An attack need not be widespread and systematic but only either wide-spread or systematic. Systematic attack is one carried out pursuant to a preconceived policy or plan. The systematic character of the attack is the guideline provided for the individual perpetrators as to the envisaged object of the attack, namely, the group of victims. For a widespread attack a larger number of victims is required than for a systematic attack. From the proved charges against the appellant there is no doubt that the appellant is responsible for systematic attacks and as well as widespread attacks.

 

395. From the charges, evidence adduced, both documentary and oral, by the prosecution and discussions made above, we are of the view that the appellant forming his own bahini, namely, "Qaiser bahini" committed widespread and systematic attacks upon civilian populations and committed offences of murders, extermination, confinement, torture, looting and arsoning. He also abetted, facilitated, added and contributed of killing, arsoning, rape and other inhumane activities of Pakistan army which are the crimes against humanity as defined in Section 3(4) of the Act. Offences, committed by the "Qaiser bahini" and Qaiser himself were widespread, systematic and those were deliberate attacks on civilian population and civilian properties. The foregoing crimes against the civil population were sufficiently appalling. The crimes against humanity upon civilian populations in the hands of the appellant and his Qaiser bahini has been proved in the greatest detail before the Tribunal. It was an unprecedented crimes against humanity committed by the appellant and his bahini during our great war of liberation. Some of the crimes stated above were committed in a most cruel, inhuman, brutal, grotesque, diabolical, revolting and dastardly manner, where the appellant's act affected the entire moral fibre of the society. The crimes committed by the appellant were immensely abhorrent, ghastly and indignant. The International Crimes Tribunal rightly convicted the appellant and sentenced him to death.
